transcript.text:
A warm fridge is often caused by simple things like a wrong temperature setting, food blocking the air vents, or dust on the coils at the back or underneath. It could also be a door seal letting warm air in, or a blocked defrost drain causing ice to choke the airflow. To help narrow this down, please check that no holiday or eco mode is active and ensure nothing is pressed against the internal vents. Also, run your fingers along the rubber door seals to see if they are torn, folded, or not closing flat.
[Helpful to see: image "Fridge not cooling — simple checks first" — Before suspecting the sealed system, check the temperature setting, that the door seal closes cleanly, that there's air space and clean condenser coils at the back, and listen for the compressor. Unplug before cleaning at the back. A sealed-system or refrigerant repair is a job for a qualified engineer. Typical layout — your model may differ.]
settings are 3 and -19, nobody's changed them. seals look fine, doors close ok. moved food from the back, no difference. freezer still freezing though

Since those basic checks didn't fix it, we need to identify the specific model to find the right part or procedure. Please look for a sticker inside the fridge, usually on a side wall near the salad drawer, and tell me the make and model number. If you can't reach the label right now because the door is stuck or something else is in the way, that's fine and we can wait until it's accessible.
[Panel: "To check a suitable replacement — Enter your model number below. Once we have the model I can check whether a suitable replacement is available. It's usually on a sticker inside the door or around the frame, or on the back of the appliance."]
Samsung. sticker says RB34 but the rest is rubbed off. no burning smell or tripping btw

Since the freezer is still freezing but the fridge isn't cold, it's likely an airflow issue rather than a complete cooling failure. The most common cause for this specific symptom on Samsung models is a blocked defrost drain at the bottom of the back wall inside the fridge compartment. Please switch off and unplug the appliance for safety, then gently clear any blockage from that small drain hole using warm water or a soft pipe cleaner. Let me know if you find ice blocking it or if clearing it helps restore cold air to the fridge section.
where's the drain? not sure where to look. there's a lot of frost on the back wall of the freezer though, more than ive ever seen

The drain hole is located at the bottom of the back wall inside the freezer compartment, usually just above the crisper drawers where any melted water would collect before draining away. Given the heavy frost you've seen on the back wall, this strongly suggests a defrost system fault that has allowed ice to build up and block airflow to the fridge section. The safest next step is to perform a full manual defrost by switching off and unplugging the appliance for 24 hours with both doors open to let all the ice melt completely. Please ensure you place towels down to catch the water and move any perishable food into cool bags during this time, then let me know once it's dry and switched back on.
ok will try the defrost. got somewhere to put the food for a day. will report back

That sounds like a solid plan and will help confirm whether it's just ice blocking the airflow. Once you've done the full defrost, switch it back on and let it run for 24 hours to see if the fridge section starts getting cold again. If the frost returns quickly after that, it points towards a failed part in the automatic defrost system like the heater or thermostat. Please let me know how it performs after you've switched it back on.
did the defrost, towels down, 24h. fridge got cold again within a day, was 3. but about 5 days on its starting to creep up again

The fact that the fridge gets cold initially after a defrost but then slowly warms up again suggests that the cooling system itself is working, but the automatic defrost cycle isn't clearing the ice as it should. This usually points to one of three components failing: the defrost heater, the defrost thermostat (thermal fuse), or the control board managing the timing. Since you've already confirmed the drain and seals are fine, we can narrow this down by checking if there is a fan running inside the freezer that pushes cold air into the fridge section. Please listen carefully when the compressor starts up to see if you hear a faint humming or whirring sound from behind the back panel of the freezer, which would indicate the evaporator fan is working.
can hear a faint scraping/ticking noise from the freezer sometimes. motor runs a lot too. not sure about a hum from the back panel

Before you start, switch it off and unplug it. The scraping or ticking noise you hear often happens when ice builds up around the evaporator fan blades and they start to hit them as they spin. This suggests that there is likely still some hidden ice blocking the airflow, which means the defrost system isn't working correctly even after your manual clear-out. Since this is a Samsung RB34, the most common cause for this recurring frost and noise is a failed defrost heater or a blown defrost thermostat (thermal fuse). To check if you can see these parts safely, we would need to remove the back panel inside the freezer compartment, but that requires switching off and unplugging the appliance first. Would you feel comfortable removing that interior panel to inspect the heating element and the small round sensor attached to the coil?
no, can't take the back panel off, no idea how and don't want to snap the clips. is there anything else I can check?

Since you can't remove the panel and have already done a full defrost with no lasting improvement, we are looking at a failed component in the automatic defrost system rather than something you can easily check yourself. The most likely causes for this recurring frost and warming fridge on your Samsung RB34 are a faulty defrost heater or a blown defrost thermostat (thermal fuse). These parts prevent the ice from melting automatically during the cycle, which eventually chokes the airflow to the fridge section. Because these components require removing the interior panel and testing with a multimeter, this is best handled by a qualified engineer who can replace the specific failed part safely.
